title: Unexpected stabilization of a single-$q$ charge density wave in pristine 1T-TiSe$_2$
authors: Kimoon Higashihira Han, Dongju Hwang, Dongsin Kim, Yeojin Ahn, Jaehun Cha, Seonggeon Gim, Gyubin Lee, Mingi Jho, Chan-young Lim, Sae Hee Ryu, Chris Jozwiak, Aaron Bostwick, Eli Rotenberg, Jonathan D. Denlinger, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Young Woo Choi, Gil Young Cho, Yeongkwan Kim
abstract: Over the past decade, studies revisiting the classical charge-density-wave system 1T-TiSe$_2$, long understood to host the $2 \times 2$ triple-$q$ order with equivalent subcomponents, have suggested that these subcomponents may not be identical, challenging a 50-year-old paradigm. Here, we demonstrate not only that these subcomponents are non-identical but also that they develop sequentially rather than simultaneously. By tracking folded-band features, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that a unidirectional $2 \times 1$ single-$q$ order stabilizes first, while the other two components emerge sequentially at lower temperatures, completing the triple-$q$ phase. Our free-energy analysis explains this hierarchy through repulsive coupling among the three subcomponents, as supported by first-principles calculations incorporating phonon anharmonicity. Consequently, the three subcomponents are inequivalent in both phase and amplitude. These results reconcile reported symmetry breaking and differing characteristic temperatures and establish a framework in which ostensibly simple, high-symmetry charge-density order emerges from temperature-dependent competition and cooperation among inequivalent subcomponents.
summary: This work re-evaluates the CDW state in 1T-TiSe$_2$, showing that the previously assumed simultaneous triple-q order is incorrect. Using ARPES and theoretical modeling, the authors demonstrate that the CDW order develops sequentially through distinct single-q phases. This sequence is explained by repulsive interactions between the constituent CDW components, providing a refined understanding of symmetry breaking in correlated materials.
main_problem: The paper challenges the long-standing paradigm of a simultaneous $2 	imes 2$ triple-$q$ charge-density wave (CDW) order in 1T-TiSe$_2$, demonstrating that the three symmetry-related subcomponents are non-identical and develop sequentially.
main_result: The CDW order emerges in a temperature-dependent sequence: a single-$q$ component stabilizes first, followed by the other two components at lower temperatures, driven by repulsive coupling between the subcomponents.
method: The study combines Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements with first-principles DFT calculations and Landau-Ginzburg free-energy analysis.
model_or_system: The physical system is the layered transition-metal dichalcogenide 1T-TiSe$_2$. The theoretical framework involves modeling the CDW order parameter using a Landau-Ginzburg free energy functional that accounts for coupling between three distinct wave vectors.
key_observables: Folded-band features observed via ARPES at specific M points ($	ext{M}_1, 	ext{M}_2, 	ext{M}_3$), spectral weight evolution, and the temperature dependence of the CDW order parameters.
important_parameters: The nature of the coupling (repulsive vs. attractive) dictates the phase sequence; the transition temperatures ($T_{	ext{CDW}}, T^*$) are key diagnostic points.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Landau-Ginzburg free energy form and incorporates phonon anharmonicity into the first-principles calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the sequential appearance of folded bands at different M points across varying temperatures, and phase diagrams comparing predictions based on attractive versus repulsive CDW interactions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first presenting ARPES evidence for sequential transitions, then using free-energy analysis to model this sequence based on repulsive coupling, and finally supporting this mechanism with detailed first-principles calculations incorporating anharmonic phonons.
why_interesting: The concept of emergent, temperature-dependent order arising from competing interactions (repulsive coupling) is highly relevant to understanding complex many-body ground states in correlated materials, which shares conceptual links with phase transitions in quantum many-body systems.
